Fleet debrief

How the boats compared, and what each can improve.

Hover any chart for the numbers behind it; drag to zoom, double-click to reset.

Fall Regatta 2026 · J/24s: Sat 14 Nov, 2 races

  • Two tracked boats, WR and Kud, on windward–leeward courses in the north bay, with the wind about 260–275° magnetic and oscillating. Race 1: W–L–W, downwind finish. Race 2: W–L, upwind finish.
  • WR finished ahead both times: by 7 s in Race 1 and by 2:43 in Race 2.
  • Where Kud's 2:50 went: 12 s at the starts, 14 s gained upwind, and 172 s lost on the runs.

What went well

  • WR: downwind speed, 0.4 kt faster than Kud at the same angle
    • Side by side on the runs, WR gained 371 m (51 lengths) in 41 minutes, 435 m (59 lengths) of it on speed.
  • Kud: upwind height, 2:00 gained on both beats of Race 1
    • Side by side upwind, Kud gained 45 m (6.1 lengths) in 22 minutes: 163 m (22 lengths) gained on course against 118 m (16 lengths) lost on speed.

Top 3 to work on

  1. Kud: downwind speed (172 s lost to WR on the runs)
    • Same heel and angle as WR, 0.4 kt slower. It's the kite, weight or steering.
    • Next time: Run beside WR and change one setting at a time until the gap stops growing.
  2. WR: upwind height (2:00 lost to Kud in Race 1)
    • Faster but lower. 18.7° of heel against Kud's 9.3° on Race 1's second beat.
    • Next time: Depower and hike before the heel passes about 12°, then point.
  3. Both: windward roundings (46–124 m (6.3–17 lengths) lost each)
    • Both boats arrived at 2.1–3.5 kt, slow next to their 4–5 kt on the beats, and took up to 90 s to settle on the run.
    • Next time: Foot into the mark, then bear away fully before the set.

Head to head

  • Race 1 changed hands at every mark. Kud won both beats, and WR won both runs and the race by 7 s.
  • Race 2 was WR's on every leg after the start, even though Kud won the start at the pin.

Data notes

  • Velocitek .vtk logs, GPS and orientation at 5 Hz. Speeds are over ground. No wind sensor on either boat.
  • Kud's line pings were 23–26 m downwind of the real line. The start lines, marks and finishes were estimated from the tracks and corrected by hand.
  • Only these two J/24s were tracked: this is not the race result.

Side by side

Every stretch where two tracked boats sailed within 500 m of each other on the same leg and the same tack or gybe.

The regatta

How this worksWhat counts as a stretch, and how the gain is split into speed and course
  • A stretch counts when two boats are within 500 m on the same leg and the same tack or gybe for at least 60 s, starting 20 s after a mark or a tack or gybe.
  • Both boats have the same wind, so what one gains is the boats: speed, and course: height on a beat (pointing against footing), depth on a run (soaking against heading up), and not sailing past the laylines.
  • Gain is distance to sail to the mark, from the GPS tracks: inside the laylines that's rungs up the ladder (sailing lower loses rungs), and past a layline the straight line back to the mark, so overstanding counts against the boat. Laylines and rungs come from the boats' own tacking and gybing angles on that leg. The split into speed and angle is from each boat's average SOG and how much of each metre it sailed brought the mark closer.
  • Watch plays the stretch on that race's replay.

Wind and current

The wind through each race from all the boats' tracks, and which side paid; then the current: COG against heading, NOAA's tide and current, and whether the water changed VMC across the course.

The regatta

ShiftsHow each boat played the shifts on the beats

Playing the shifts, every beat

  • Sat 14 Nov: 25 shifts of 4° or more on the beats, 20° typical, a full swing about every 3 min.
BoatOn the lifted tackTacks on a headerHeaded before tacking (median)Sailed headed (1 min or more at a time)
Kud46%4 of 1284 s12:35

Lifted and headed are against the wind's average over the last few minutes (8, centred), within 2° counts as neither. 50% on the lifted tack is what tacking at random gets. Not every tack should be on a header: laylines, lanes and covering come first, and near a layline the headed tack is often the one that gets to the mark.

Current

CurrentCOG against heading, NOAA's tide and current, and VMC across the course

What COG − heading is made of

The gap between course over ground and heading adds up three things: the compass offset (the same on every heading), leeway (upwind, to leeward) and current. Without a paddlewheel, current running along the wind can't be told apart from leeway, so upwind the two are reported together as slip. Between boats in the same water, a difference in slip is a difference in leeway. Current across the course can be measured, and so can where the set was stronger.

Tack to tack: speed and drift

A current across the course makes one tack faster over the ground and the other slower, and pushes both tracks the same way. Comparing port with starboard on the same leg, for the same boat, takes the compass out of the speed test completely (each boat's compass is calibrated differently). Real current shows up on every boat, holds from a beat to the run after it, and agrees with the drift. Waves or pressure on one tack don't.

Each dot is one boat on one leg: its median SOG on starboard minus port (steady sailing only). Circles: beats; diamonds: runs. Hover for the current across the course each would imply, and what the drift says.

Tide and current from NOAA

Tide

Current at the station

Across the course: NOAA's prediction against what the boats measured

Shaded: the races. The line is the station's current resolved across the course (+ toward the right side, looking upwind); the dots are each boat's fit for each race, at mid-race. NOAA's current up and down the course can't be checked this way (it looks like leeway), so it's in the hover only.

Upwind and downwind, port and starboard

Median COG − heading, compass offset removed. + means the boat tracked to the right of its heading. Upwind, the gap between port and starboard is twice the slip.

Leg by leg

Each dot is one boat on one tack or gybe of one leg (20 s or more of steady sailing). If both tacks move the same way from one beat to the next, the water changed; if they move apart, the slip did.

Left or right, bottom or top: did the current change VMC across the course?

The course is split into nine zones: left, middle and right of the line from the leeward gate to the windward mark (150 m either side is the middle), and its bottom, middle and top thirds. Each zone shows VMC (speed toward the mark) against the boat's own average in that race, and how much of that the water explains. Water running down the course (measured from slip on the beats) takes that speed off VMC on a beat and adds it on a run. The rest is wind and sailing. Values are knots; ± is the noise.

The course

Upwind is up the page. Cells are coloured by the median of every sample in them from the boats and races selected; faint cells have few samples. Hover a cell for its numbers. Drag to zoom, double-click to reset.

Numbers from analyze.py and fleet.py. Speeds are over ground. Times are local to the event.
